In addition, the government of Singapore would also look into Asia Pulp & Paper which was incorporated in Singapore and First Borneo Plantations which has ownership links to Singaporean-incorporated companies.

=== Indonesia-Singapore Cooperation on Transboundary Haze ===
In October and November 2026, Indonesia and Singapore announced two initiatives to strengthen cooperation in addressing transboundary haze caused by forest and land fires in Indonesia: the establishment of a bilateral task force; and the development of the ASEAN Coordinating Center for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control in Indonesia.

==== Indonesia-Singapore Bilateral Task Force ====
On 27 October, Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir and Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan agreed to establish a bilateral task force to investigate companies suspected of involvement in illegal land burning. The cooperation would include information sharing, tracing financial transactions and cross-border corporate relationships, and strengthening law enforcement. The initiative would complement Indonesia's existing enforcement efforts, which had resulted in legal action against hundreds of individuals and more than 50 companies, while Singpore had issued preventive notices to 10 companies.

==== ASEAN Coordinating Center for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control ====
On 3 November 2026, Singapore's Minister for Sustainability and the Environment, Grace Fu, announced plans to advance the establishment of the ASEAN Coordinating Center for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control in Indonesia during Singapore's ASEAN Chairmanship term in 2027. The center aims to strengthen regional coordination in preventing and combating forest fires, including information sharing, technology exchange and emergency assistance. The establishment of the center would require ratification of the agreement by at least 6 ASEAN member states.

title: 2026 London Marathon
text:
The 46th London Marathon took place on 26 April 2026. The race was the third of seven World Major Marathon events and was a platinum label race. The route featured three separate starting points — one by Greenwich Park and two on Blackheath common — and ended on The Mall. Notable landmarks en route included Cutty Sark, Tower Bridge, Canary Wharf and Buckingham Palace. The race was historic for several reasons: it was the first marathon completed in under two hours, with Sabastian Sawe achieving a time of 1:59:30. The elite men's runner-up, Yomif Kejelcha, also finished the race in under two hours (1:59:41), recording the fastest non-winning marathon time and the fastest marathon debut in history. Third-place finisher Jacob Kiplimo also finished under the previous world record. In the women's elite field, Tigst Assefa set a new world record for a women-only marathon. Additionally, many national records were set for both men and women, such as Peter Lynch's 2:06:08 for Ireland, and Julia Paternain's 2:25:47 for Uruguay.

== Planning ==
The women's race was originally announced to include Olympic champion Sifan Hassan and world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir, but both runners withdrew due to injury, leaving Tigst Assefa, Joyceline Jepkosgei, and Hellen Obiri as the headliners. Tigst said in the pre-race press conference that she was fitter than she was last year, when she won the race and set a 2:15:50 women's-only world record.
In the men's race, the debut of Yomif Kejelcha was highly anticipated as the Ethiopian was coming off both a successful track career and several fast half marathon performances. Sabastian Sawe, the defending champion, was viewed as trustworthy given that he had voluntarily subjected himself to increased drug testing paid for by his sponsor Adidas in the lead-up to the race. However, he revealed during the pre-race press conference that he had been dealing with a back injury before the race. 5,000 m and 10,000 m world record holder Joshua Cheptegei was also entered in the race, but he had struggled in his three career marathons before London.
The event received 1,133,813 ballots for entry. It was a new world record for entrants to a marathon, surpassing the 840,318 applications from the 2025 London Marathon.

== Elite races ==

=== Men ===
By five kilometres into the men's race, a group of six runners had separated from the rest of the pack. Sawe, the defending champion, was joined by Paris Olympic champion Tamirat Tola, world cross country champion Jacob Kiplimo, marathon debutant Yomif Kejelcha, Deresa Geleta, and Amos Kipruto. They were led by a group of pacers through the half marathon in one hour and 29 seconds, aligned with the 60:30 target pace.
The pacers were able to block the wind until after 25 kilometres (16 mi), at which point Sawe sped up (contrary to expectations that runners would run faster when behind a pacesetter). 29 kilometres (18 mi) into the race, only Sawe and Kejelcha remained in the lead with Kiplimo trailing. At 30 kilometres (19 mi), the pair was still only at a projected 2:01 finish, but Sawe split a 13:54 5K run from 30 to 35K to bring the pace down to 2:00:29. Sawe's 24th mile time of 4:12 was the fastest individual mile split recorded in any marathon, but Kejelcha remained in contact with the lead. On 1 May, an analysis showed that the 4:12 24th-mile split for Sawe was likely inaccurately measured, and London's official timing company mika:timing removed the split from their data.
Kejelcha was finally dropped after the 25th mile, leaving Sawe by himself as he ran the stretch from 40 km to 42.195 km in 5 minutes and 51 seconds. Both Sawe and Kejelcha broke the two-hour marathon barrier, while Kiplimo broke the previous world record time of 2:00:35 in 3rd place. All of the top five runners ran a personal record time over the marathon distance.

=== Women ===
In the women's race, former marathon world record holder and defending champion Tigst Assefa broke away from the elite field early along with Hellen Obiri, Joyciline Jepkosgei, and Catherine Reline Amanang'ole. Obiri was primarily known for her performances on slower marathon courses like the Boston Marathon and New York City Marathon and was debuting on the London course, while Jepkosgei was the 2021 London Marathon winner.
By 15 kilometres (9.3 mi), only Tigst, Obiri, and Jepkosgei remained. They ran the half marathon in 1:06:12, half a minute faster than Tigst's split the previous year and only two minutes slower than the 1:04:16 split run during Ruth Chepngetich's 2:09:56 mixed-gender world record run.
The trio slowed in the following miles, running every 5 km split after 20 km in over 16 minutes. Nonetheless, Tigst maintained the pace enough to break her own women's-only world record by nine seconds, finishing in 2:15:41. Obiri and Jepkosgei also ran under 2 hours and 16 minutes, marking the first time that three women had broken the 2:16 barrier in the same race.

== Reception ==
A total of 59,830 runners finished the race, setting a new Guinness World Record for the largest marathon and beating the 2025 New York City Marathon's 59,226 finishers. Though not yet officially announced, the 2027 London Marathon had been rumoured to be the first World Marathon Major to separate into two races held over two days to accommodate larger crowd sizes. An estimated 800,000 spectators attended the race live in London.

== Participant data ==
The 2026 London Marathon finishers had a gender split of 59.7% men and 40.1% women. Among the general participants the average finish time was 4:36:28, the fastest age group being those aged 40-44. 68% of finishers were from the United Kingdom.  88 year old Harry Newton was the oldest participant, with a total of 37 people over the age of 80 entered in the race. 

== Results ==
Sawe set a world record in the men's marathon, and Tigst set a world record for a women-only marathon.

=== Elite runners ===

=== Elite wheelchair ===

== Charity ==

The 2026 London Marathon featured several runners dressed in costumes, running for charitable causes, while others were raising awareness of illnesses. Patrick Barkham finished the race in a badger costume to raise funds for wildlife conservation and in memory of his late father. Fiona Betts finished the race in a helicopter costume in support of air ambulance services. Jonathan Acott, a cancer survivor, attempted to break a world record while dressed as a knight in armour, while raising funds for his charity. Other participants dressed up in costumes such as a polar bear, a two-person elephant and a giant testicle costume. 
A costumed Daddy Pig from Peppa Pig ran the marathon to raise money for the National Deaf Children's Society. He was coached by, and ran alongside, Joe Wicks. YouTuber Dawko ran the marathon while dressed as the character Freddy Fazbear from Five Nights at Freddy's to raise money for the Samaritans.

title: February 2026 New Zealand storms
text:
In mid-February 2026, a wet weather system brought heavy rain, flash flooding and land slips to parts of New Zealand's North and South Islands. States of emergency were declared in the Ōtorohanga, Waipā , Tararua, Manawatū, Rangitīkei Districts and Banks Peninsula. Plane, ferry, train and road travel were disrupted in several districts in both islands. One man was killed after his car was submerged at Puketotara on State Highway 39 on 14 February.

== Preparations ==
On 13 February 2026, MetService issued an orange heavy rain warning for the Bay of Plenty east of Ōpōtiki and the Gisborne District north of Tolaga Bay. A yellow heavy rain warning was also issued for the rest of the North Island. That same day, the Hastings District Council issued an evacuation order for residents of the Clifton Motor Camp's campground near Cape Kidnappers due to a high landslide risk.

== Timeline ==
During the week leading up to 19 February 2026, the Wellington Region, the Manawatū-Whanganui east and north of Palmerston North, the Waikato region between Palmerston North and the Coromandel Peninsula, the eastern Northland Region, Bay of Plenty, Hawke's Bay and Gisborne District in the North Island experienced rainfall totals of 50 to 100 mm. In addition, the ranges and foothills of the central North Island experienced 100 to 200 mm of rain during that week. Other parts of the North Island including Taranaki, the western Waikato, the Auckland Region, the western Northland Region, and the rest of Manawatū-Whanganui experienced between 10 and 30 mm of rainfall during that week.
In the South Island, Christchurch, the Banks Peninsula, the northern Canterbury Region and the Southern Alps of the Westland District experienced rainfall totals of 50 to 100 mm during the week leading up to 19 February. Other areas including parts of Otago between Dunedin and Balclutha, the Canterbury high country, Fiordland and much of the Westland District south of Greymouth experienced rainfall totals of 30 to 50 mm. During that seven-day period, the rest of the South Island recorded rainfalls of less than 30mm.

=== North Island ===
On 14 February, 80 people were evacuated following flash flooding in the Ōtorohanga District. A local state of emergency was also declared. Many road and highways in the district were flooded. The body of a man was also recovered from a submerged car at Puketotara on State Highway 39.
On 14 February, the Waipā District also experienced heavy rain and flash flooding, leading to a local state of emergency.
On 15 February, a state of emergency was declared in the Tararua District in response to flash flooding. Red heavy rain warnings were also issued in the Manawatū, Rangitikei and Ruapehu Districts. That same day, states of emergency were declared in the Manawatū and Rangitīkei Districts in response to heavy rain and flash flooding overnight.
On 17 February, flash flooding in the Manawatū–Whanganui led to another local state of emergency being declared. 

==== Wellington Region ====
On 15 February, stormy weather also caused the cancellation of several Interislander and Bluebridge ferry services across the Cook Strait. 
On 16 February, the Wellington Region experienced strong winds, leading to the cancellation of all Wellington train services in the morning and numerous flights. A train collision with a fallen tree also disrupted travel near Wairarapa the previous day. On 16 February, 30,000 properties in the Manawatū–Whanganui and Wellington regions experienced power outages due to strong winds toppling trees and power lines. Local authorities also evacuated several homes in Masterton due to the threat of fallen trees. On 16 February wind speeds of up to 193 kilometres per hour (120 mph) were recorded at Mount Kaukau and 128 kilometres per hour (80 mph) were recorded at Wellington Airport. The last time winds that strong were recorded in those areas was in 2013. The suburb of Kelburn had a maximum southerly wind speed of 133 kilometres per hour (83 mph), which was the highest wind speed the area experienced in that direction in over a decade. At 7am a wind gust of 240 kilometres per hour (150 mph) was recorded in the Wairarapa. On the night between 15 and 16 February, the Wairarapa experienced 256.4 millimetres (10.09 in) of rainfall, Wellington experienced 121 millimetres (4.8 in) and the Tararua District recorded 101.9 millimetres (4.01 in).
On 17 February flooding also destroyed a single-lane bridge in the southern Wairarapa district, isolating several local settlements including Lake Ferry, Ngawi and Whāngaimoana. The Wellington City Council made green waste disposal at the Southern Landfill free for a week following 19 February due to garden damage caused by the storm. Some homes in the south coast of Wellington were coated with spray that may have contained faecal matter, blown by the wind after about a billion litres of raw sewage had been dumped into the ocean near Moa Point due to a wastewater treatment plant failure. Wellington Water said at the time that the spray might have just been uncontaminated salt spray.
On 20 February, a landslip rendered a hillside home in the Lower Hutt's Stokes Valley uninhabitable. On about 20 February, Wellington Zoo created a fundraising campaign to care for birds swept up by the storm. These birds included albatrosses, penguins and petrels. A vet at the zoo said that they had been "overwhelmed" by the amount of birds needing treatment, and were running out of space for them.
On 23 February, 300 homes in Wellington, Porirua and the Hutt Valley were still without power. The storm also caused a large amount of driftwood to appear along several kilometres of Paekākāriki beach, with one resident stating that "there's no sand, it's just all logs and then mulch".

=== South Island ===
On 14 February, the Christchurch City Council issued a boil water notice for several eastern Christchurch suburbs due to bacteria contamination in the Rawhiti water supply zone caused by heavy rain. On 15 February, heavy rain warnings were also issued for Banks Peninsula and the Canterbury Plains.
On 16 February State Highway 75 was closed between Tai Tapu and Akaroa due to flooding. 
On 17 February, Banks Peninsula and Christchurch also experienced heavy rain and flash flooding, leading to a state of emergency being declared in the former. A boil water notice was issued in Wainui after the local water supply was contaminated by flooding.
On 18 February, a landslip in Dunedin's Musselburgh suburb led to the evacuation of seven hillside properties on Belmont Lane. One of these properties was subsequently rendered unsafe and classified as "red stickered."
On 21 February, 40 Student Volunteer Army volunteers from the University of Canterbury assisted Civil Defence and the Taskforce Kiwi volunteers in clearing up silt and flood damage in the Banks Peninsula.
On 23 February, the state of emergency in the Banks Peninsula was lifted by Mayor of Christchurch Phil Mauger. That same day, Christchurch City Council controller Duncan Sandeman confirmed that three properties in Banks Peninsula had been red-stickered and that two more had been yellow-stickered.

title: Alaskan Party
text:
The Alaskan Party (AP) is an Alaskan nationalist political party in the United States. The Alaskan Party is intended to be a successor to the defunct Alaskan Independence Party (AIP), which dissolved in December 2025. Former AIP chair Bob Bird and vice chair Mark Chryson founded the Alaskan Party in March 2026.

== History ==

In December 2025, board members of the Alaskan Independence Party voted to dissolve itself, citing declining membership. Party chair John Wayne Howe claimed that the party drifted from its original purpose following the death of its founder, Joseph E. Vogler, in 1993. In the announcement of its dissolution, AIP officials called the party "legally alive yet spiritually dead". Howe also believed many members of the party registered as AIP members under the false assumption that they were registering as independents. Former chair Bob Bird opposed the dissolution, wanting a convention to reconstitute the party. Bird and former vice chair Mark Chryson met with Attorney General Stephen J. Cox and Lieutenant Governor Nancy Dahlstrom in March to postpone the dissolution, but were unsuccessful.
The Alaskan Party was registered with the Alaska Division of Elections in March 2026. The Alaska Division of Elections reported the Alaskan Party had 22 registered members as of May 2026, doubling to 44 members by September 2026. Per state law, the Alaskan Party is recognized by the state as a political group, with 5,000 members required in order to be recognized as an official political party.
One candidate ran for office under the Alaskan Party in 2026, former Unalaska City Council member Earl D. "Skip" Southworth, who ran for U.S. Senate against incumbent Republican senator Dan Sullivan. Alaska Beacon and Anchorage Daily News reported that the Wisconsin-based super PAC Right For Alaska spent $219,000 promoting Southworth's campaign, in an attempt to act as a spoiler against Sullivan's candidacy. Alaska Beacon discovered FEC reports from a Dutch Harbor resident named Earl Southworth, who previously donated to the Kamala Harris presidential campaign in 2024 and a state senate campaign for Democrat Forrest Dunbar. Southworth failed to advance past the jungle primary, placing ninth among a field of sixteen candidates, with 0.5% of the total vote.

== Positions ==
The Alaskan Party shares similar positions with the preceding Alaskan Independence Party. The party does not call for Alaskan secession, but advocates for an in-state referendum that would include the option of Alaska becoming an independent country. The party maintains the 1958 statehood vote was flawed and lacked options for becoming a commonwealth or total independence from the United States, unlike statehood referendums for other U.S. territories like Puerto Rico. The Alaskan Party also opposes federal ownership of Alaskan land, claiming it makes Alaska dependent on the federal government.
In an op–ed published by the political blog The Alaska Story, party co–founder Bob Bird stated that the Alaskan Party would be sympathetic towards voters who want "limited government and constitutionally recognized rights," including disaffected Republicans and Libertarians.

title: Salvadoran military intervention in Haiti
text:
Since 21 October 2026, El Salvador has been conducting a military intervention in Haiti following a gang ambush on 18 October that resulted in four Salvadoran aviation technicians of the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) being kidnapped. According to Salvadoran president Nayib Bukele, the intervention's primary objective is to rescue the four technicians, while threatening to "finish" the Haitian gangs if the technicians are not rescued alive.
A gang conflict has engulfed Haiti since 2020 with gangs taking control of much of the country, including most of the capital, Port-au-Prince. In 2023, the United Nations Security Council established the Multinational Security Support Mission (MSS, later reorganized as the GSF) to help the Haitian government combat gangs. El Salvador began supporting the GSF in January 2025 in non-combat roles and had at least 124 personnel in Haiti by October 2026. After Haitian gangs attacked and kidnapped the four Salvadoran technicians, Bukele announced the beginning of a military operation to rescue them. Salvadoran troops began arriving in Haiti on 22 October, since November, El Salvador has deployed 2,000 to 2,500 soldiers to Haiti, and more than the 1,500 GSF troops in Haiti. Salvadoran troops began conducting search and rescue operations on 30 October. On 8 November, a joint operation involving Salvadoran forces destroyed a house belonging to Wilson Joseph—the leader of the 400 Mawozo gang—that was allegedly the gang's headquarters. According to Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, at least 100 people have been killed during the intervention as of 11 November 2026.
Haitian forces and the GSF are directly supporting the Salvadoran intervention. Furthermore, the United States, Colombia, and the Dominican Republic have provided El Salvador logistical support in transporting Salvadoran personnel and equipment to Haiti. Most Salvadoran troops in Haiti are operating independently from the GSF. Some analysts have accused the intervention of being an invasion, which both Bukele and Haitian prime minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé deny. According to a CID Gallup opinion poll, the majority of Salvadorans approve of the intervention; Haitian civilians have protested in support of the intervention, with some protesting against it under threat of gang violence. Joseph has called for the United Nations to mediate peace talks between El Salvador and the gangs, which the Salvadorans have rejected.

== Background ==
In May 2020, Haitian gangs launched several attacks in various neighborhoods of Port-au-Prince, the capital city of Haiti, to secure and expand their territory. Since then, a gang war has engulfed much of Haiti. After the 2021 assassination of Jovenel Moïse, the president of Haiti, gangs expanded their control and influence throughout Haiti, some of which had connections to political parties. By June 2023, gangs controlled most of Port-au-Prince and thousands had died due to gang-related violence. In October 2023, the United Nations Security Council established the Multinational Security Support Mission (MSS) at the request of the Haitian government to provide peacekeeping in the country.

In March 2024, Salvadoran president Nayib Bukele remarked that his government could solve the gang war in Haiti. Since 2022, Bukele's government had overseen a nationwide crackdown on gangs in El Salvador resulting in 78,175 arrests by March 2024. On 30 October 2024, the Legislative Assembly of El Salvador approved a decree that authorized the deployment of Salvadoran military personnel to Haiti until October 2026 to support the MSS with medical evacuations. On 3 January 2025, El Salvador deployed eight Salvadoran Air Force personnel to Haiti, and in February 2025, it deployed a further 70 soldiers. In October 2025, the UN Security Council reorganized the MSS as the Gang Suppression Force (GSF). On 29 September 2026, the Legislative Assembly extended El Salvador's involvement in the GSF until October 2027. By then, El Salvador had at least 124 personnel in Haiti supporting the GSF.
From January to September 2026, over 5,700 people were killed or injured due to gang-related violence in Haiti, with a further 230 people kidnapped and 1,000 being raped. By October 2026, hundreds of gangs operated in Haiti, with some organized into large gang alliances such as G9 Family, Viv Ansanm, and G-Pèp. The International Crisis Group estimates that Viv Ansanm alone has 12,000 to 20,000 members. According to InSight Crime, the Haitian National Police (PNH) receives little supervision from the Haitian government leading to members allegedly engaging in criminal activity, with some PNH members supposedly having ties to gangs. Furthermore, the GSF was understaffed, only having 1,500 soldiers out of the 5,500 expected by autumn 2026.

== Kidnapping of Salvadoran technicians ==

On 18 October 2026, Haitian gang members attacked an armored vehicle carrying four Salvadoran aviation technicians attached to the GSF in Croix-des-Bouquets (a commune near Port-au-Prince) with explosives while they were returning to base. The four technicians fled the destroyed vehicle but at some point later, gang members kidnapped the four technicians and took them hostage. No group has been officially identified as being responsible for the ambush nor has any group claimed responsibility. 
Egriselda López and Mike Waltz, the respective Salvadoran and American ambassadors to the UN, condemned the attack and called for an international mission to rescue the technicians. The GSF and PNH conducted a helicopter offensive against gangs in Plaine du Cul-de-Sac near where the technicians disappeared, killing several gang members and injuring four GSF personnel.

== Chronology of the intervention ==

=== Deployment ===
On 21 October, Bukele wrote on X that gang members were holding the technicians as hostages and announced the beginning of a military operation to rescue them. In Bukele's X post, he wrote that the mission's sole goal was to rescue the four technicians alive and unharmed. He, however, threatened the Haitian gangs that if the technicians were not rescued alive, he would "finish" them like he "already finished with the gangs in El Salvador" ("nou deja fini ak gang yo nan El Salvador").  Bukele addressed the post directly to Haitian gang leaders. After Bukele's announcement, the GSF told La Prensa Gráfica that the operation involved ground units supported by helicopters. In a statement, the Haitian prime minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé announced that the Haitian government intends to assert its authority over armed groups and that the release of the technicians was an "absolute priority".
On 22 October, El Salvador deployed 100 special forces soldiers to Haiti to assist in the search and rescue operation. By 28 October, the Salvadoran government stated that it had 2,000 troops deployed in Haiti, surpassing the GSF's 1,500 troops in Haiti. Since November, sources have varyingly reported that El Salvador has 2,000 to 2,500 soldiers in Haiti. El Salvador also deployed five MD Helicopters MD 500E and two Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters to participate in the rescue operation and to transport troops and supplies. The United States Southern Command (USSOUTHCOM) and the Colombian Aerospace Force helped transport El Salvador's soldiers to Haiti onboard Lockheed C-130 Hercules aircraft. Furthermore, the Dominican Republic helped facilitate the transport of Salvadoran personnel and equipment through its territory. Dominican president Luis Abinader stated that the country would assist El Salvador with logistics and intelligence.
On 29 October, Bukele wrote on X that the Salvadoran government was covering 90 percent of the costs of the intervention and that the deployment of soldiers and supplies to Haiti was nearly complete. He added that all Salvadoran forces would withdraw when the intervention concluded. Bukele later stated in a press conference that, if the gangs return the four technicians, all Salvadoran forces would leave Haiti immediately. On 16 November, Salvadoran justice minister Gustavo Villatoro reiterated that all Salvadoran troops would withdraw from Haiti once the technicians were recovered. Haitian justice minister Patrick Pélissier, with whom Villatoro was meeting, stated that Fils-Aimé wanted to expand the scope of the Salvadoran mission beyond the recovery of the technicians.
In response to the deployment of Salvadoran troops to Haiti, Krisla, a gang leader, published a video acknowledging that the GSF has "bigger weapons and more technology" than the gangs but that "we'll fight to the end". He added that "we didn't ask Bukele to come here, and we didn't ask Bukele to send soldiers here. Bukele has come here to protect his money at his soldiers' expense." Wilson Joseph, the leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, posted a video showing off ammunition saying that he would wait for the Salvadorans to arrive and that he would not flee the country.

=== Operations and patrols ===
On 30 October, Salvadoran troops conducted their first operation of the intervention when dozens of troops conducted patrols in Tabarre. There, they established a base of operations near the US embassy. Gang members fired gunshots at a Salvadoran convoy near the embassy the following day. On 2 November, Salvadoran troops in armored vehicles advanced into Plaine du Cul-de-Sac, reportedly killing at least a dozen 400 Mawozo and Chèn Méchan gang members. The PNH and GSF supported the Salvadorans in the operation. That day, the PNH recovered the destroyed armored vehicle that transported the four kidnapped technicians in Croix-des-Bouquets.

On 3 November, Fils-Aimé expressed support for the Salvadoran intervention and reiterated that the Haitian government intends to assert its control over all Haitian territory. He stated that the PNH and Armed Forces of Haiti (FAd'H) would join the GSF and Salvadoran forces to form in a "common strategy" against the gangs. That night, Salvadoran helicopters repelled gang members in Croix-des-Bouquets who launched an attack against Chadian GSF soldiers. On 5 November, Mathias Saintil, the leader of the Boston gang, was killed in Cité Soleil by a loitering munition (self-destructing military drone) in an operation conducted by the PNH, the GSF, Task Force (a mercenary group founded by Erik Prince), and El Salvador. Saintil was the first Haitian gang leader to be killed in a military operation since 2024.

On 8 November, Salvadoran helicopters and a Task Force loitering munition launched an airstrike that destroyed a house belonging to Wilson Joseph (400 Mawozo's alleged headquarters), killing up to 20 gang members. The operation came days after Bukele asked users on X to identify the location of Joseph's home so that he could "destroy it". On 11 November, Fils-Aimé stated that the Salvadoran intervention was helping the Haitian government regain control of territory. The following day, Salvadoran troops and armored vehicles—along with personnel from the PNH, FAd'H, and Task Force—established a base inside the Sylvio Cator Stadium in downtown Port-au-Prince, which had previously been controlled by gangs since 2024. Bukele told gang members to leave the area or face "consequences" in a future military operation. On 18 November, Salvadoran helicopters destroyed a house in Canaan belonging to Jeff Larose, the leader of the Taliban gang, but it is unknown if Larose was killed. The GSF did not participate in the attack, and it is unclear if Haitian forces were involved.

=== Calls for mediation ===
On 1 November, Joseph asked the United Nations to mediate peace talks between El Salvador and the gangs, claiming to want a "peaceful solution to the national crisis". On 6 November, a 400 Mawozo spokesperson told the Associated Press (AP) that the gang was ready to enter peace negotiations and undergo disarmament in exchange for an end of "international interference" in Haiti. Salvadoran vice president Félix Ulloa rejected considering UN mediation with the gangs, describing it as "unacceptable".

== Casualties ==
Doctors Without Borders reported that 30 civilians were wounded by gunfire or explosions in Port-au-Prince between 18 and 26 October. Haitian civilians have also reported heavy gunfire and drone strikes possibly resulting in civilian deaths. At some point before 10 November, US chargé d'affaires to Haiti David Howell stated that three Salvadoran soldiers had been injured and that one had to be medically evacuated back to El Salvador. The Salvadoran government denied Howell's report and accused him of spreading false information. According to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) non-governmental organization (NGO), over 100 people have been killed during El Salvador's intervention, at least 26 of whom were civilians, as of 11 November 2026.
On 28 October, United Nations Association – Haiti (UNA–Haiti), an NGO  that represents the Haitian diaspora, condemned El Salvador's intervention and demanded a UN investigation into its conduct. UNA–Haiti wrote a letter to António Guterres, the UN secretary-general, accusing the Salvadorans of carrying out aerial bombardments and helicopter attacks resulting in civilian deaths in Croix-des-Bouquets. Bukele criticized UNA–Haiti's statement, denying that Salvadoran forces deployed bombs and asserted that their helicopters arrived after the statement was published.

== Impact on Haitian politics ==
The Haitian government announced on 29 October 2026 that it would hold presidential and legislative elections in July 2027, with a second round in October if necessary. The elections will be the first held in Haiti since November 2016. The elections' conduct is partly reliant on the Salvadoran intervention improving the country's security, as the elections were previously scheduled to occur in December 2026 but the government postponed them due to gang violence. Jean-Marie Théodorat, the director of the Department of Geography at the University of Paris, told France 24 that the intervention opened a "window of opportunity" ("fenêtre d'opportunité") for Haiti to hold elections.

== Analysis ==

=== Legality ===
Sandra Pellegrini of ACLED questioned if Salvadoran forces would act outside of the GSF's jurisdiction in Haiti. She stated that operation parallel to the GSF could "undermine the legitimacy of the international mission to suppress the gangs" ("debilitar la legitimidad de la misión internacional de supresión de las pandillas"). Günther Maihold, a Latin American studies professor at the Free University of Berlin, raised concerns that the intervention could be against international law if operating outside of the GSF.
On 2 November 2026, UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric stated that the majority of Salvadoran troops are operating outside of the GSF's jurisdiction. According to Dujarric, the Salvadoran intervention is a bilateral matter between El Salvador and Haiti. The following day, Fils-Aimé stated that Salvadoran troops were "not here to replace the state" but to support Haitian and GSF troops fighting the gangs. He added that the Haitian government was responsible for what foreign troops were present in the country. While Salvadoran troops attached to the GSF report to GSF commander Major General Erdenebat Batsuuri, those sent as a part of the intervention are commanded by Salvadoran colonel José Roberto Figueroa Amaya. Amnesty International has called for El Salvador and Haiti to disclose the terms of the Salvadoran deployment. On 16 November, Ulloa stated that the terms of the deployment would not be disclosed until "diplomatic conditions permit that it be public" ("condiciones diplomáticas lo permitan para hacerlo público") but that the deployment was nonetheless "legitimate".
Romain Le Cour, the head of the Haiti Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, questioned the framework of the Salvadoran chain of command and its rules of engagement. He also called for scrutiny on the extent of the United States' involvement in the intervention. Some critics accused the intervention of being an invasion or occupation, which Bukele, Fils-Aimé, and Ulloa denied.

=== Mission outcome ===

Maihold told Deutsche Welle that the gang situations in El Salvador and Haiti are not comparable. He stated that the Salvadoran gangs largely did not put up an armed resistance to Bukele's crackdown, and contrasted that situation to Haiti where gangs are more extensive and have deeper connections to security forces. Le Cour noted that many Haitian prisons were largely emptied in 2024 and that the judicial system is ineffective which would make implementing a Salvadoran-style crackdown difficult. Former Pentagon official Francisco O. Mora told The Economist that the Salvadorans may face difficulties as Bukele "does not know the terrain or the tactical environment".
Vanda Felbab-Brown, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, has speculated that if there are heavy civilian casualties or the intervention becomes prolonged, the Salvadorans could be seen by the Haitians as an invading force. José Miguel Cruz, a criminology professor at the Florida International University, predicted that the security situation in Haiti would worsen as a result of the intervention. He argued that it would cause backlash from both the gangs and from Haitian civilians who would perceive the intervention as a violation of Haiti's national sovereignty. Théodorat speculated that the Salvadorans found more success in combating Haitian gangs than previous missions such as United Nations Stabilization Mission in Haiti (deployed from 2004 to 2017) as they have directly confronted the gangs militarily and could have an "empathetic ideal" to help Haiti.

=== Geopolitical implications ===
Le Cour stated that the Salvadoran intervention could set a regional precedent where a country could withdraw from international missions to alter their rules of engagement. He added that if the Salvadoran intervention is a quick success, Bukele "will evolve from being the architect of a prison model to an actor capable of conducting military interventions beyond his own borders" ("pasaría de ser el promotor de un modelo carcelario a un actor capaz de intervenir militarmente fuera de sus fronteras"). Frances Robles, a contributor for The New York Times, similarly wrote that a successful intervention could boost Bukele's international standing "as the leader who pulled Haiti out of crisis when other nations either refused to help or were incapable". Robert Muggah, a co-founder of the Igarapé Institute, wrote that the intervention is "the first overseas test of Bukele's security model". He added that, because El Salvador is a member of the US-led Shield of the Americas, other members could become involved as a part of anti-transnational crime cooperation.
Salvadoran historian Carlos López Bernal described the use of the Armed Forces of El Salvador in the intervention as being political in nature. He compared it to the 2003 to 2009 deployment of the Cuscatlán Battalion during the Iraq War, when Salvadoran presidents Francisco Flores and Antonio Saca sought to politically support the US. Adam Isacson, a security specialist at the Washington Office on Latin America, speculated that Bukele wants the intervention to boost his anti-crime reputation ahead of the 2027 Salvadoran presidential election. Muggah wrote that Salvadoran casualties could lead to domestic criticism ahead of the election and pressure a further escalation.

== Reactions ==

=== Haiti ===

On 2 November, Haitian civilians in Plaine du Cul-de-Sac protested against the Salvadoran intervention under death threats from Viv Ansanm. In contrast, Edwin Paraison, a former consul of Haiti to the Dominican Republic, told reporters that the majority of Haitians support the intervention. Jean-Baptiste Elysée, the leader of the Independent Patriotic Voice (VIP) political party, expressed support for the intervention. Thousands of Haitians have marched in support of the intervention in several Haitian cities such as Belladère, Jérémie, Kenscoff, and Port-au-Prince, with some calling on the Salvadorans to extend their operations to other parts of the country.

=== El Salvador ===

Salvadoran journalist Leonel Herrera accused Bukele of launching the intervention in Haiti as propaganda to supposedly improve El Salvador's image and distract from economic conditions in El Salvador. Manuel Zometa, a lawyer, demanded government transparency on how the intervention is being funded. Rafael Aguirre, the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front's presidential candidate in the 2027 election, remarked that the intervention was a "show" and an "unnecessary war". Bukele has responded to criticism of El Salvador's intervention on X by affirming his confidence that the gangs would be defeated and that God would grant the Salvadorans victory.
According to an opinion poll conducted by CID Gallup from 24 to 27 October, 86 percent of Salvadorans approved of the rescue mission in Haiti, but 82 percent also worried about the risks that Salvadoran personnel faced while carrying out the mission. Additionally, 51 percent had high confidence that the technicians would be rescued alive. Furthermore, 68 percent supported maintaining or increasing involvement in Haiti, and 73 percent believed that El Salvador's involvement in Haiti improved the country's image abroad.

=== United States ===
US president Donald Trump supported the Salvadoran deployment during a phone call with Bukele on 27 October, telling him "do what you have to do". Trump stated that the US would not supply El Salvador with equipment, however, remarking that "he [Bukele] doesn't need help". While Trump has expressed support for El Salvador, he also suggested that the four technicians may be dead. According to Axios, Bukele made a proposal to Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, to increase El Salvador's role in combating gangs in Haiti with US materiel support as a sort of proxy. Rubio reportedly declined the offer, wanting to "keep Haiti off the radar". Rubio later told reporters that the Salvadorans should work in conjunction with the GSF to avoid friendly fire during anti-gang operations.
On 4 November, Howell told Fils-Aimé to order Salvadoran defense minister René Merino Monroy to halt operations until Salvadoran troops can coordinate with the GSF, fearing that they could kill GSF troops or civilians. The following day, the US embassy in San Salvador sent a formal complaint to the Salvadoran government denouncing a "lack of coordination" between El Salvador and the GSF. It also claimed that Salvadoran small arms fire hit the US embassy and almost injured a staffer. Bukele criticized Howell and the complaint, remarking that "[Trump] told me to do what we have to do, and now a bureaucrat is opposing it?" Salvadoran foreign affairs minister Alexandra Hill Tinoco stated that Salvadoran and GSF forces were already in coordination.
Irwin Stotzky, a human rights expert at the University of Miami, speculated that the US could be invested in the intervention's outcome as the Trump administration ended temporary protected status for 350,000 Haitians in the US earlier in 2026. Stotzky stated that the Trump administration wants to "make it appear as if it's safe to send 350,000 people back to Haiti".

=== Other countries ===
On 19 October, Guatemala deployed 50 soldiers to Haiti to join the GSF, one day after the ambush against the Salvadoran technicians. On 24 October, the Dominican Republic deployed 10,000 soldiers along its border with Haiti to reinforce it amidst the escalation of El Salvador's intervention in Haiti. José Ignacio Paliza, the Dominican minister of the presidency, stated that the Dominican government would "take the necessary steps to protect our integrity" should anything occur along the border.

title: 2026 EUT20 Belgium
text:
The 2026 EUT20 Belgium was the inaugural season of the EUT20 Belgium, a professional men's Twenty20 cricket league in Belgium. The tournament featured five franchise teams representing Belgian cities. The competition was played from 6 to 14 June 2026 in a single round-robin format, followed by the Playoff league and the final.
The final was held on 14 June 2026, when the Ghent Gladiators defeated the Antwerp Anchors by 3 wickets to win the inaugural title. Ali Khan of the Ghent Gladiators was awarded the man of the match award for his match-winning performance, while JJ Smit of the Antwerp Anchors was named player of the tournament.

== Background ==
The league was established in late 2025 to professionalise cricket in Europe, with former England captain Eoin Morgan serving as the global brand ambassador. All matches were played at the Stars Arena in Zemst, near Brussels. Zemst is a municipality located in the province of Flemish Brabant, Belgium.

=== Format ===
The 2026 EUT20 Belgium season followed a franchise T20 format featuring five teams.
The league stage was played in a single round-robin format, with each team playing the others once for a total of 10 matches. Following this stage, the fourth and fifth-placed teams contested a qualifying match, with the winner securing the final spot in the playoff league.
The top four teams then advanced to the Playoff league, which was played in a single round-robin format with six matches, and the top two teams qualified for the final to decide the champion.

== Draft and personnel signings ==

=== Draft ===
The player draft for the 2026 season took place on 24 March 2026.
Teams acquired players through a centralized player draft. Each squad, consisting of 16 to 18 members, had to follow strict roster requirements:

Domestic: 4 Belgian players (minimum 2 in the starting XI; compulsory for every squad).
Associate: 4 players from ICC Associate nations.
International: 4 active Full Member international players.
Veterans: 6 Full Member players who had not played international cricket in the last two years.

=== Personnel signings ===
Each franchise had a salary budget of approximately £183,000 ($250,000), with individual player contracts ranging from £1,500 to £22,000 ($2,000–$30,000).
Ahead of the draft, several high-profile international stars were confirmed as pre-signings.
West Indies all-rounder Sheldon Cottrell, Bangladeshi all-rounder Shakib Al Hasan, South African batter Rilee Rossouw, and English internationals Jason Roy and Alex Hales were announced as pre-signings for Akcel United Brussels.
West Indies all-rounder Andre Russell, New Zealand international Martin Guptill, and South African players Hardus Viljoen, Delano Potgieter, and Wihan Lubbe were pre-signed by the Antwerp Anchors.
South African internationals Temba Bavuma, Dwaine Pretorius, and all-rounder Duan Jansen along with English international James Vince, and Australian batter Josh Brown were pre-signed by the Ghent Gladiators for the inaugural season of the tournament.
South African internationals Rassie van der Dussen, and Wayne Parnell, New Zealand international Colin Munro, Nepalese all-rounder Dipendra Singh Airee, and Indian all-rounder Nikhil Chaudhary were announced as pre-signings for JB Bruges.
United States all-rounder Corey Anderson, Pakistani all-rounder Shoaib Malik, Australian batsman Chris Lynn, Nepali leg-spinner Sandeep Lamichhane, and South African batter Faf du Plessis were pre-signed by the Liège Red Lions ahead of the inaugural season.

== Teams ==
The following five franchises were confirmed for the inaugural season.

== Squads ==
The following squads were confirmed for the inaugural season of the EUT20 Belgium.

Crishan Kalugamage and Matthew Cross, who were acquired by the Ghent Gladiators during the draft, were later removed from the squad in the team's new announcement on 10 May 2026, and were replaced by Ali Hasan and Ali Khan on 20 May and 21 May 2026, respectively. The franchise also announced the signings of Bernard Scholtz and JJ Smuts on 6 June 2026, as supplementary additions to the squad.
Lokesh Bam was signed by the Antwerp Anchors as a replacement for Saad Nawaz. On 1 June 2026, the franchise announced that Aasif Sheikh would be unavailable due to national team commitments at the Asian Games – Men's Qualifier. Later that day, the team also announced the signings of Tom Moores, JJ Smit, and Peter Hatzoglou as supplementary additions to the squad, even after the conclusion of the player draft. On 6 June 2026, Moeen Ali was also added to the team.
Akcel United Brussels announced the signings of Danru Ferns, Jack Jarvis, Thomas Draca, Dale Phillips, and Thomas Rogers as supplementary additions to the squad even after the conclusion of the player draft.
Liège Red Lions announced the signings of Hayden Kerr, Shaaron Lewis and Murid Ekrami as supplementary additions to the squad even after the conclusion of the player draft.
Despite not being officially announced in the initial squad, Jack Wildermuth was seen playing for JB Bruges in their match against the Ghent Gladiators.
